newsitem.title: USA: Police probe Calif. fire for homicide clues.
newsitem.headline: Police probe Calif. fire for homicide clues.

text.p: Detectives probing a fire that swept through a California house, killing nine people, said Sunday the blaze was suspicious in origin and they had started a homicide investigation.

Don O'Keefe, a detective sergeant with the San Mateo County Sheriff's Office, said Saturday's blaze in East Palo Alto, 50 miles south of San Francisco, was suspicious and arson was a possibility, but no definite cause had yet been established.

He said investigators gathered samples from the carport -- where they believe the fire started -- and the interior of the house and sent them to a local forensic laboratory to find out if the samples contained an accelerant -- such as gasoline or kerosene.
Officials were waiting to get the results back from the lab before they could say conclusively what caused the fire.
Because the fire was suspicious, "we're treating it as a homicide investigation until we know different," O'Keefe said.
O'Keefe said detectives were still busy interviewing relatives and neighbours, but had no information about any possible grudge against the family.
Five children, aged between five and 11, and four women all from the same family, died in the early-morning fire, authorities said.

The children were staying with their grandmother, 78-year-old Verna McKean, who escaped from the burning house. She was released from a local hospital Saturday after treatment for respiratory problems. Two adults and a child remained in a hospital being treated for burns or smoke inhalation.
Victims were trapped inside the house by burglar bars bolted on the windows. The bars are common in the neighbourhood, which has a high crime rate.

Firefighters had a hard time getting into the building because a burning car blocked access to the front door and two angry pit bull dogs barred their way when they tried to go around to the back of the house.

Capt. Harold Schapelhouman, a spokesman for the Menlo Park Fire District, said late Saturday that investigators had eliminated all possible natural causes of the fire. He said there were "strong suspicions there may be foul play involved."
The San Mateo County Sheriff's Department asked for the public's help and said people could call a 24-hour hotline if they had information about the fire.
Menlo Park Fire District Chief Rick Tye said it was the deadliest fire in the district's 80-year history.
